studies.title: Grant reviewers quietly favour scientists from their own country — and the bias is bigger than gender bias
studies.ns_score_reason: Very large dataset, counterintuitive finding that nationality bias outweighs gender bias in science funding, strong societal hook around fairness and scientific meritocracy, clean design with multiple reviews per application — minor deductions for observational design and single-funder scope.
studies.the_study: Economists analysed 37,073 applications for European Research Council grants, each receiving multiple independent reviews, to test whether shared nationality, citizenship, or gender between reviewer and applicant influenced scores. Reviewers who shared an applicant's country of work or citizenship awarded significantly higher scores than those with no such match, with the effect largest when both country of work and citizenship aligned. Shared gender also increased scores, but to a smaller degree than country-based homophily. Correlational panel-level analysis further found applicants were more likely to advance past the first evaluation stage when the panel chair or more panel members shared their country.
studies.why_it_matters: Because grant funding shapes which science gets done and whose careers advance, systematic nationality-based bias in peer review could skew the direction of global research and entrench inequalities in who succeeds in academia.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "Where you're from matters more than your gender when it comes to winning research grants" An analysis of over 37,000 European Research Council applications finds that reviewers systematically score applicants from their own country higher — an effect larger than the well-documented gender bias in science funding. Science prides itself on judging ideas, not people. But a sweeping new analysis of 37,073 ERC grant applications shows that reviewers quietly favour applicants who share their nationality or citizenship — awarding them meaningfully higher scores, regardless of the proposal's content. The effect is strongest when reviewer and applicant share both country of work and citizenship, and it is larger than the already-concerning gender homophily in grant review. The finding raises urgent questions about whether international peer review, long seen as a safeguard against parochialism, is actually reproducing national hierarchies in science. Why it fits: NS Mind readers care deeply about fairness, institutional bias, and the social forces that shape whose ideas get heard — this finding cuts right to the heart of scientific meritocracy.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center. Observational design only — causation cannot be established; data from one funder (ERC) may not generalise to other grant systems or regions; authors were paid contractors for the ERC, which should be disclosed as a potential conflict of interest even though the data access arose from that role *Editor's fact-check note: N=37,073 confirmed from abstract. 'Single-center' flag applied because data comes from one funding body (ERC) only, limiting generalisability to other grant systems. Industry/conflict-of-interest flag noted: authors were contracted experts for the ERCEA and were compensated for this work, though they conducted the study as a direct product of that engagement — this should be disclosed in any article.*

studies.title: People who use pornography to escape — not just to cope — show more problematic patterns, but the heaviest users sit in the middle
studies.ns_score_reason: Counterintuitive finding (mid-profile users consume most pornography, not high-profile) in a decent-sized human sample with a clear societal hook around trauma, sexuality, and mental health — strong NS Mind fit despite self-report and single-site limitations.
studies.the_study: Researchers surveyed 608 young adults (ages 18–27; 73% men) in Israel, measuring compensatory and dissociative pornography use patterns, childhood trauma, impulsivity, loneliness, and emotion regulation. Latent profile analysis identified three user profiles (Low, Mid, High). Unexpectedly, participants in the Mid — not the High — profile reported the highest overall pornography consumption, while those in the High profile showed the most severe psychological symptoms. Childhood sexual abuse severity was significantly associated with greater problematic pornography use and higher consumption frequency.
studies.why_it_matters: The counterintuitive finding that the heaviest consumers cluster in a middle — not extreme — psychological profile suggests that frequency of use and psychological harm do not map onto each other as simply as previously assumed, which could inform how clinicians screen for problematic use.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "The heaviest pornography users aren't the ones with the worst mental health — it's more complicated than that" You might expect the people in the most psychological distress to watch the most pornography, but a new study finds the opposite: the heaviest consumers sit in a psychological middle ground. A study of 608 young adults finds that when researchers sorted people by their motivations for watching pornography — using it to feel better (compensatory) versus using it to feel nothing (dissociative) — those with the most severe symptoms didn't watch the most pornography. Instead, a middle group consumed pornography most frequently, while the high-symptom group reported more loss of control and distress despite lower overall consumption. Separately, childhood sexual abuse severity was linked to both more problematic use and higher consumption. The findings suggest that raw viewing time is a poor proxy for psychological harm. Why it fits: NS Mind readers are drawn to findings that upend intuitive assumptions about behaviour, especially where sex, trauma, and mental health intersect.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: self-reported outcomes, observational design, single-center, small female subsample (27% women). All data are self-reported; sample is 73% male, limiting conclusions about women; study conducted at a single Israeli university, so findings may not generalise; cross-sectional design means no causal conclusions can be drawn *Editor's fact-check note: Age SD reported in abstract as 4.8 but mean is 24.3 — plausible for a university sample. Female representation noted as a caveat given only 27% women in sample. No industry funding disclosed. Study conducted in Israel — noted in summary.*

studies.title: So-called 'causal illusions' may not be irrational after all — they reflect our prior beliefs updating on new evidence
studies.ns_score_reason: Strongly counterintuitive — reframes a well-known 'cognitive bias' as rational inference — with a large combined sample, clean experimental design, and a clear hook for readers interested in superstition, conspiracy thinking, and how humans learn.
studies.the_study: Researchers ran four experiments with 1,860 participants to test why people sometimes perceive a causal relationship where none exists — a phenomenon traditionally labelled an irrational 'causal illusion.' By experimentally manipulating participants' prior causal beliefs either through visual mechanism information or statistical base-rate information, they found that lowering those priors reduced how strongly people reported a causal link after seeing non-contingent data. The results aligned with a Bayesian model of causal learning, suggesting what looks like a cognitive bias is actually rational updating of prior beliefs when evidence is weak or ambiguous.
studies.why_it_matters: Reframing 'causal illusions' as rational Bayesian inference rather than cognitive bias has broad implications for understanding superstitious thinking, conspiracy beliefs, and why corrective information sometimes fails to dislodge false cause-and-effect beliefs.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "Seeing causes that aren't there isn't a bias — it's your brain doing rational maths" What psychologists have long called a cognitive illusion — believing a sugar pill cures your cold, or that your lucky socks won the match — may actually be a sign your brain is working exactly as it should. Four experiments involving nearly 1,900 people found that the famous 'causal illusion' — perceiving a cause-and-effect relationship where none exists — shrinks or grows depending on what participants already believed before seeing the data. That's exactly what a rational Bayesian brain should do: weigh new evidence against prior knowledge. The finding challenges decades of framing these illusions as straightforward cognitive failures, with provocative implications for superstition, pseudoscience belief, and why telling people the facts doesn't always change their minds. Why it fits: NS Mind readers are fascinated by challenges to established ideas about irrationality, and this finding directly reframes a textbook cognitive bias as sensible Bayesian inference.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: laboratory/experimental paradigm with limited ecological validity, single-country sample (Germany). All experiments used controlled laboratory tasks that may not mirror real-world causal learning; sample appears to be drawn from a single country (Germany); the Bayesian framing, while supported, is one theoretical interpretation and not universally accepted in the field *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirms N=1,860 across four experiments; direction of effect (lower priors → weaker causal illusion) verified against abstract. No corrections needed.*

studies.title: Your bad mood makes you cling to negative thoughts — and those thoughts make your mood worse
studies.journal: Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science
studies.ns_score_reason: Strong counterintuitive finding (emotions drive thoughts more than thoughts drive emotions), decent human sample with preregistered design, clear relevance to depression and anxiety — topics NS Mind readers care deeply about.
studies.the_study: Researchers at Tilburg University and KU Leuven developed a novel smartphone-based task — the Daily Life Interpretation Inflexibility Task (DL-IIT) — and embedded it in a 14-day ecological momentary assessment protocol. Community adults (N=179) with varying levels of depression and social anxiety completed 12,950 surveys tracking their momentary interpretations and emotions in everyday life. The study found that emotion-to-cognition pathways were actually stronger than cognition-to-emotion pathways: negative moods predicted greater subsequent persistence of negative interpretations more robustly than sticky negative thoughts predicted worsening mood. Higher symptom severity amplified these mood-congruent feedback loops.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests that targeting emotional states directly — not just thought patterns — may be at least as important in breaking self-reinforcing cycles of distress, which has implications for how clinicians think about sequencing psychological interventions.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "Your bad mood drives negative thinking more than your thoughts drive your mood" We're often told that challenging negative thoughts will lift our mood — but a new study tracking people's minds in real time suggests the arrow of influence points the other way. Using a novel smartphone-based task delivered across 14 days, researchers tracked how negative interpretations and emotions influenced each other moment to moment in 179 community adults. Contrary to the standard cognitive model, they found that feeling bad predicted clinging to negative interpretations more strongly than negative interpretations predicted worsening mood — and the effect was amplified in people with higher depression or anxiety symptoms. The finding raises questions about whether 'think your way out of it' advice is putting the cart before the horse. Why it fits: NS Mind readers are fascinated by how cognition and emotion interact, and this directly challenges the cognitive-primacy assumption that underpins much popular mental-health advice.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, community sample may not generalise to clinical populations. Observational design means causality cannot be confirmed; community sample may not reflect clinical severity; self-reported emotions and interpretations; study conducted in Belgium/Netherlands, cultural generalisability worth noting *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirmed N=179, 14-day EMA, 12,950 completed surveys. Direction of effect (emotion→cognition stronger than cognition→emotion) verified against abstract. No corrections needed.*

studies.title: Reduced placebo pain relief in autism is actually explained by alexithymia, not autism itself
studies.journal: Autism: The International Journal of Research and Practice
studies.ns_score_reason: Directly overturns a prominent prior belief about autistic perception, decent human sample with careful group comparisons, strong neurodiversity hook, though small N and single-center are notable caveats.
studies.the_study: Researchers in London and Oxford recruited 96 adults — including 28 autistic people, 25 alexithymic people, and 55 non-autistic, non-alexithymic controls — and used a placebo hypoalgesia paradigm to manipulate expectations about pain relief from electric shocks. They found that alexithymia and trait anxiety reliably predicted how much the placebo effect reduced perceived pain, while any effect of autism was small and unreliable. The results suggest that differences in pain perception previously attributed to autism may actually stem from co-occurring alexithymia.
studies.why_it_matters: This finding challenges a widely held theoretical account of autistic perception and suggests that decades of pain-related research conflating autism with alexithymia may need reinterpretation, with implications for how pain is assessed and managed in autistic people.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "The reason autistic people seem less susceptible to placebo pain relief is not autism — it is alexithymia" A leading theory holds that autistic brains process pain differently because they rely less on top-down expectations — but a new study suggests the real culprit is something else entirely. Researchers tested whether autistic adults were less influenced by placebo suggestions of pain relief, as prior theory predicted. They found autistic traits barely mattered — but alexithymia, the difficulty identifying and describing one's own emotions, strongly predicted how much the placebo worked. The finding adds to mounting evidence that a generation of autism research may have been measuring the wrong thing. Why it fits: NS Mind readers are fascinated by how autism research is being reappraised, and this study adds to a growing body of evidence that alexithymia — not autism per se — explains many observed differences.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center. Small sample (N=96) limits statistical power; single-centre UK study; alexithymia and autism groups were not matched on all variables — journalist should note these as preliminary findings requiring replication

studies.title: Anxiety and intolerance of uncertainty feed each other in a vicious cycle through the teen years
studies.ns_score_reason: Large longitudinal human sample, counterintuitive bidirectional finding that overturns a common assumption (that uncertainty intolerance is a simple precursor to anxiety), strong topic fit for NS Mind mental health and adolescence coverage — docked one point for self-report measures and single-country sample.
studies.the_study: Researchers followed 3,562 Chinese adolescents (mean age 14.27 years at baseline; 55.4% girls) across three time points to examine whether intolerance of uncertainty causes internalising symptoms (anxiety, depression) or results from them. Using cross-lagged panel models and random-intercept cross-lagged panel models, the study found that the relationship is bidirectional — not only does intolerance of uncertainty predict subsequent rises in internalising symptoms, but worsening internalising symptoms also predict subsequent increases in intolerance of uncertainty, even at the within-person level after controlling for stable individual differences.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding that uncertainty intolerance and anxiety mutually reinforce each other across adolescence suggests that intervening on either target — not just one — may be important for breaking the cycle in teenage mental health.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "Teen anxiety and fear of uncertainty make each other worse in a feedback loop" A large longitudinal study finds that intolerance of uncertainty doesn't just cause adolescent anxiety — anxiety also makes teens less able to tolerate uncertainty, creating a self-reinforcing cycle. Most research has treated intolerance of uncertainty as a risk factor that predisposes young people to anxiety and depression. A new three-wave study of over 3,500 teenagers now shows the relationship runs in both directions: not only does struggling with uncertainty predict worse mental health later, but deteriorating mental health also makes teens less tolerant of uncertainty. The study used sophisticated statistical methods to show this isn't just because anxious teens are a different type of person — the feedback loop operates within the same individual over time. The finding suggests that targeting either anxiety or uncertainty-intolerance in therapy may help break the cycle. Why it fits: With adolescent mental health at the top of the public agenda, this finding reframes how we think about what drives teen anxiety and what to do about it.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes. Observational longitudinal design (no causal inference), self-reported measures, conducted entirely in China so cultural generalisability is uncertain, single institution *Editor's fact-check note: Sample size N=3,562 confirmed from abstract. Study conducted in China (South China Normal University); generalisability to other cultural contexts should be noted. No small-sample flag needed (N well above 100). Longitudinal design is a strength but not an RCT, so observational flag retained.*

studies.title: Smoking scars from housing hardship linger long after people find stable homes
studies.ns_score_reason: Large US longitudinal cohort, counterintuitive asymmetry finding with clear societal hook around housing insecurity and addiction — strong fit for NS Mind.
studies.the_study: Using longitudinal data from 12,965 young adults in the US National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health, researchers tested whether entering and exiting housing hardship had symmetrical effects on smoking, binge drinking, and marijuana use. Asymmetric fixed-effects models revealed that entering housing hardship was associated with increased smoking frequency, but leaving hardship was not associated with a corresponding reduction — consistent with the persistence of nicotine dependence. Binge drinking and marijuana use showed more reversible, symmetric responses to housing transitions, and hardship-related increases in smoking and marijuana use were more pronounced among men.
studies.why_it_matters: Housing assistance programmes may not automatically reduce smoking rates even when they successfully stabilise people's living situations, suggesting that addiction support needs to be integrated into housing interventions.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "Getting out of housing hardship doesn't undo the smoking it caused" Securing stable housing reduces stress — but it doesn't reduce the smoking habit that housing hardship triggered, new research suggests. A study of nearly 13,000 young Americans found that falling into housing hardship increased smoking frequency, but finding stable housing again did not bring smoking back down — a stark asymmetry not seen for binge drinking or marijuana use. The finding, explained by nicotine's particularly tenacious grip, suggests that housing policy alone cannot undo the addictive harms of housing precarity. With housing insecurity rising in many countries, the implication is that social support programmes need to pair housing with tailored addiction treatment. Why it fits: NS Mind readers care about the social determinants of mental health and behaviour, and the intersection of poverty and addiction is highly topical.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes. Observational design means causality cannot be established; self-reported substance use; US-based sample (Add Health) may not generalise to other countries with different housing markets and welfare systems

studies.title: Brief phone calls from non-specialists dramatically boost completion of digital binge-eating therapy
studies.journal: The International Journal of Eating Disorders
studies.ns_score_reason: Strong topic fit for NS Mind (mental health treatment access, eating disorders), counterintuitive angle that non-specialist brief calls rival specialist therapy engagement, but heavily penalised by very small N, no control group, and single-arm design.
studies.the_study: Oxford researchers ran a single-arm mixed-methods pilot study with 19 adults experiencing recurrent binge eating, testing a fully remote digital CBT-E programme augmented by brief audio support calls from non-specialist supporters. Programme completion was 79% (15 of 19 participants completed all 12 sessions), substantially higher than typical digital intervention dropout rates. Among completers, large effect-size improvements in binge eating frequency, eating disorder psychopathology, and clinical impairment were observed at both post-programme and 6-month follow-up.
studies.why_it_matters: Eating disorders are severely undertreated partly because specialist therapist time is scarce; this early evidence suggests that adding minimal, non-specialist human contact to digital programmes could substantially improve engagement and outcomes, pointing toward a scalable access solution.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "A non-expert making short phone calls could be the key to digital therapy actually working" Just five minutes of audio support from a non-specialist — not a therapist — was enough to keep nearly 80% of binge-eating patients completing a 12-session digital programme, far outpacing typical dropout rates. Digital CBT programmes promise to democratise mental health treatment, but most people quit before finishing them. Oxford researchers tested whether adding short, informal audio calls from untrained supporters could change that — and found completion rates that rival face-to-face therapy. The twist is that the callers weren't therapists; they were non-specialists providing accountability and encouragement, suggesting the human ingredient in therapy may be simpler than we thought. Why it fits: NS Mind readers care about mental health access and the real-world limitations of digital therapy — this study reframes what 'support' in treatment actually needs to look like.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, no control arm (single-arm pilot), self-reported outcomes, short follow-up (6 months), preprint status not confirmed but online ahead of print. Tiny pilot study of just 19 people with no control group, so it's impossible to say how much of the improvement came from the support calls versus the programme itself; all outcomes self-reported; conducted at a single UK centre *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract states N=19 enrolled, 15 completed assessments (79% completion). Qualitative interviews conducted with n=13 and satisfaction survey with n=11 — these sub-group sizes noted. No control group; this is a single-arm pilot. Summary and caveats reflect this accurately.*

studies.title: Hearing someone use singular 'they' makes you more likely to use it yourself — and also boosts use of 'he' and 'she'
studies.ns_score_reason: Counterintuitive finding about how singular 'they' primes binary pronouns too, solid experimental design across two samples, strong societal hook around gender-inclusive language, though the core topic is psycholinguistics rather than mental health.
studies.the_study: Researchers at the University of North Carolina ran two priming experiments — one with college students and one with community adults aged 30–70 — to test whether hearing singular 'they' increases its subsequent use. They found that hearing singular 'they' did prime its later use, and also increased use of 'he' and 'she', suggesting activation of a broad third-person pronoun category. The effect was stronger specifically for singular 'they', and also reduced pronoun errors, pointing to both general and specific representational activation.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding the cognitive mechanisms behind adoption of singular 'they' could inform how language communities adapt to expanding pronoun norms, with implications for education, media, and workplace inclusion efforts.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "Hearing singular 'they' makes you more fluent with 'he' and 'she' too — pronouns are more contagious than we thought" Using gender-neutral pronouns does not just spread themselves — it turns out it also boosts use of gendered pronouns, revealing something unexpected about how language works in the brain. Two experiments found that simply hearing someone use singular 'they' makes listeners more likely to use it themselves — confirming that social exposure drives adoption of this relatively new pronoun use. The surprise is that the priming spills over to 'he' and 'she' as well, suggesting the brain stores all third-person pronouns in a shared cognitive category that gets activated together. The finding reframes debates about singular 'they' as a matter of cognitive architecture as much as cultural politics. Why it fits: NS Mind readers are engaged by language, cognition, and the social science of how norms spread — and singular 'they' is one of the most debated linguistic shifts of the decade.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes. Both samples are US-based, limiting cross-linguistic or cross-cultural generalisability; participants were not tested for prior attitudes to gender-neutral language, which could influence priming effects *Editor's fact-check note: The study involves two experiments, not one; Experiment 2 was pre-registered. No self-reported outcomes flag is appropriate here — removed that caveat. The design is experimental, not purely observational.*

studies.title: Cutting back on cannabis does not reliably push people toward alcohol or cigarettes
studies.ns_score_reason: Counterintuitive finding that challenges a common clinical fear about substance substitution, decent pooled sample, but effects are modest and design is observational secondary analysis.
studies.the_study: Researchers pooled data from 829 adults (mean age 27) enrolled in seven pharmacological cannabis use disorder clinical trials to examine whether reducing cannabis use prompted compensatory increases in alcohol or cigarette use. Cannabis craving combined with cannabis use frequency was associated with only modest increases in next-week alcohol quantity, while higher cannabis use predicted slightly lower subsequent cigarette use. Pharmacotherapy did not broadly alter these substitution patterns, and among those on active treatment, higher craving was actually associated with fewer smoking days.
studies.why_it_matters: The fear that treating cannabis use disorder will simply push people toward other substances has limited treatment-seeking; this study suggests that cross-substance substitution, while worth monitoring, may be more limited than commonly assumed.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "Quitting cannabis does not push people toward drinking more, data from seven trials suggest" One of the biggest fears about treating cannabis addiction — that people will simply swap one drug for another — may be largely unfounded, according to new pooled data. A study pooling 829 participants across seven clinical trials found only weak evidence that reducing cannabis use leads people to drink more alcohol, and actually found some suggestion that cigarette use decreases in tandem with cannabis use. This runs counter to a widely held clinical assumption about cross-substance substitution. The finding could reshape how clinicians counsel patients about what to expect when they seek treatment for cannabis use disorder. Why it fits: NS Mind readers are interested in addiction, behaviour change, and the practical realities of mental health treatment.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, secondary analysis. Observational secondary analysis with self-reported substance use; effects were statistically significant but small in magnitude; predominantly younger, white participants may limit generalisability

studies.title: The sound playing in your ears subtly controls what your eyes think they see
studies.ns_score_reason: Genuinely counterintuitive finding about multisensory perception with a strong attention-dependence twist; loses points for unreported N, non-preregistered design, and self-report limitation.
studies.the_study: Researchers at the University of Queensland tested whether an instinctive association between sound pitch and visual lightness — high pitch feels bright, low pitch feels dark — could tip the scales of what people perceive when their two eyes are shown conflicting images (binocular rivalry). Across three experiments with participants viewing black and white circles while hearing high or low tones, the study found that congruent sound-image pairings (e.g. white circle + high tone) biased what people reported seeing as dominant — but only when participants were directly attending to lightness, and only after sustained exposures of five seconds or more. No effect emerged when lightness was task-irrelevant. The abstract does not report total participant N across experiments.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests that the brain's multisensory associations quietly shape conscious visual experience, but only under conditions of active attention — with implications for understanding how perception is constructed from competing inputs.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "The sound playing in your ears subtly controls what your eyes think they see" When your two eyes are shown conflicting images at the same time, a tone playing in your ear can quietly tip your brain toward seeing one over the other — but only if you're paying attention. Your brain has ingrained associations between the senses — high-pitched sounds feel bright, low-pitched sounds feel dark — and a new study suggests these silent rules can nudge conscious visual perception during moments of rivalry between the eyes. The catch is striking: the effect only emerged when participants were actively focused on visual lightness, and disappeared entirely when lightness was irrelevant to the task. This points to attention as the gatekeeper of multisensory influence on what we consciously see. Why it fits: NS Mind readers love perception science that reveals how the brain quietly constructs reality from competing signals — this has a clear, demonstrable hook.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: small sample (N not reported in abstract), self-reported outcomes, study not preregistered. Participant N not reported in abstract; study not preregistered; authors themselves caution that results reflect reported rather than purely perceptual dominance; effects depended on specific timing windows and task demands *Editor's fact-check note: Total participant N is not reported in the abstract; flagged as small/unreported sample. The abstract itself cautions that findings reflect effects on reported dominance rather than definitive perceptual modulation — this nuance is preserved in the summary.*

studies.title: When asked what makes them nostalgic, people overwhelmingly reach for sensory memories — not life milestones
studies.ns_score_reason: Solid human sample and clear societal hook around nostalgia and memory, but largely confirmatory rather than counterintuitive, and observational self-report design limits impact.
studies.the_study: Researchers at Aarhus University asked 256 participants to freely describe what makes them feel nostalgic, without predefined response categories. Responses were coded for cue type, nostalgia type, content, cultural life-script events, and gender differences. Sensory and environmental cues — photographs, music, smells, food, conversations — dominated responses, while culturally scripted life events such as weddings or graduations were rarely mentioned, with childhood being the main exception. Gender differences were modest.
studies.why_it_matters: The convergence between what people spontaneously report and what experimental lab studies use as nostalgia triggers suggests sensory cues have a privileged role in autobiographical memory retrieval, with potential relevance for therapeutic and design applications.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "Nostalgia is triggered by smells and songs, not the life events you think define you" When people are asked what makes them nostalgic, they almost never mention weddings or graduations — they reach for the smell of a kitchen or a half-remembered song. A study gave 256 people a blank page and asked what makes them nostalgic. Rather than naming the big life milestones that cultural scripts say should matter, participants overwhelmingly described sensory fragments — food, music, photographs, scents. The finding challenges assumptions about how autobiographical memory works and may help explain why the past so often arrives uninvited. Why it fits: Nostalgia sits at the intersection of memory, emotion, and everyday life — a sweet spot for NS Mind readers.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 — actually N=256, no flag needed), observational design, self-reported outcomes. Observational self-report design; Aarhus University sample may skew towards certain cultural or demographic backgrounds; study describes patterns rather than testing causal mechanisms *Editor's fact-check note: Initial caveats draft incorrectly flagged small sample; N=256 does not meet the N<100 threshold, so that flag has been removed.*

studies.title: Brain stimulation boosts spatial memory — but only the first time you try it
studies.ns_score_reason: Counterintuitive null finding (anti-phase as good as in-phase) and session-decay result give it a solid hook for NS Mind's cognition-curious readers, but the unreported and likely small N, single-centre design, and niche methodology limit broader appeal.
studies.the_study: Researchers applied 6 Hz transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to the fronto-parietal network of participants in a within-subjects design across four sessions, measuring visuospatial working memory using the Corsi Block Tapping Task. Both in-phase and anti-phase stimulation improved memory accuracy compared to no stimulation, but the effect was strongest in the first session and faded over subsequent sessions. Counterintuitively, anti-phase stimulation — which disrupts rather than synchronises neural oscillations — performed no worse than in-phase stimulation, challenging the assumption that synchrony is key. No effects on response speed were found.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding that brain stimulation's memory benefits rapidly diminish with repeated sessions suggests current tACS protocols may need redesigning before they can be used reliably in therapeutic or cognitive-enhancement contexts.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "Brain zapping improves memory — but the effect vanishes after one session" A technique that uses electrical pulses to tune brain rhythms sharpened spatial memory, but only the very first time participants tried it. Scientists applied gentle alternating electrical currents to volunteers' foreheads to synchronise brain oscillations thought to underpin spatial memory — and it worked, lifting accuracy on a classic memory test. But here's the catch: the boost almost entirely evaporated by the second session, raising serious questions about whether tACS can ever be a reliable cognitive tool. Even stranger, disrupting brain rhythms worked just as well as synchronising them, upending a core assumption in the field. Why it fits: NS Mind readers are fascinated by cognitive-enhancement technologies and will be gripped by the idea that a promising brain-stimulation effect essentially disappears with practice.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, short follow-up. Sample size is not reported in the abstract and is likely small; the study is from a single lab; effects were measured over only four sessions; no long-term follow-up; results may not generalise beyond the specific task used *Editor's fact-check note: The abstract does not report the exact sample size (N), so small sample flag is applied cautiously based on a within-subjects lab design at a single institution; no industry funding is mentioned. The abstract confirms the session-dependent attenuation and the null anti-phase vs in-phase difference as reported in the summary.*

studies.title: Menu labels cut calories ordered in Indian restaurants — but only in some settings
studies.ns_score_reason: Strong RCT design with large N and a societal/policy hook, but the heterogeneous results limited to one restaurant and a South India-specific regulatory context reduce generalisability and counterintuitive punch for a global NS Mind audience.
studies.the_study: Researchers conducted a four-arm RCT across two chain restaurants in an Indian metropolitan city, recruiting 2,462 adult diners. Participants were randomised to receive menus with quantitative nutrient information, interpretational guidance, contextual guidance, or a control (unlabelled) menu. In one of the two restaurants, all three labelling formats significantly reduced calories ordered (by roughly 10–12%), and interpretational labels also reduced fat ordered; however, effects varied markedly between restaurants, and no impact on salt or sugar intake was observed.
studies.why_it_matters: With India having implemented mandatory menu labelling regulations for large restaurant chains in 2022, this trial suggests that how nutritional information is presented — not just whether it appears — may shape its real-world effectiveness, a finding relevant to global public health policy debates.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "Menu calorie labels only work in some restaurants — and nobody knows why" A large randomised trial finds that menu labelling cut calories ordered by about 10% — but only in one of the two restaurants tested, raising awkward questions about what actually drives the effect. India mandated calorie labelling on menus for large restaurant chains in 2022, and researchers finally put it to a proper randomised test with nearly 2,500 diners. The labels did reduce calorie choices — but the effect vanished entirely in one of the two restaurants studied. That unexplained inconsistency is the real story: context matters as much as the label itself, and policymakers rolling out blanket labelling rules may be surprised by patchy results. Why it fits: NS Mind readers are interested in the psychology of choice and how environmental nudges really work — this trial complicates the tidy narrative that labels change behaviour.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: single-center (two restaurants in one city), observational design for between-restaurant heterogeneity, short follow-up, study population limited to South India. Results only significant in one of two restaurants tested; study conducted in a single Indian city so generalisability to other cultural or restaurant contexts is uncertain; no long-term follow-up to assess whether ordering habits actually changed over time *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract specifies results were heterogeneous between restaurants and significant calorie reductions were only observed in Restaurant 2, not both. Summary reflects this stratification accurately. Study is an RCT so causal language is appropriate for the intervention effect within the trial.*

studies.title: Most patients become briefly confused after electroconvulsive therapy — but nearly all recover within 30 minutes
studies.ns_score_reason: Clinically relevant RCT on a stigmatised but highly effective psychiatric treatment, with a somewhat surprising delirium prevalence figure, but small N, single-centre, and partial blinding limit its strength for NS Mind.
studies.the_study: In a prospective randomised trial at a tertiary care centre in Kota, India, 90 adult patients undergoing electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) were allocated to one of three anaesthetic agents — propofol, etomidate, or thiopental (n=30 each). Delirium was assessed at 15 and 30 minutes post-ECT using validated scales. Post-ECT delirium occurred in 72.2% of patients at 15 minutes, but 83.1% of those had recovered by 30 minutes; longer seizure duration was independently associated with higher delirium odds, while thiopental and etomidate were associated with significantly lower delirium odds than propofol.
studies.why_it_matters: ECT remains one of the most effective treatments for severe depression, and understanding which anaesthetic agents are associated with reduced post-procedure confusion could help clinicians manage a common and distressing side effect — though larger trials are needed before any practice changes.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "Seven in ten patients briefly lose mental clarity after electroconvulsive therapy — but most recover within half an hour" Post-ECT confusion is far more common than many patients are told — but it is also far more fleeting, according to a new randomised study. A randomised trial of 90 patients found that nearly three-quarters experienced delirium in the 15 minutes following ECT — a rate higher than often cited in patient information materials. But 83% of those had fully recovered within 30 minutes, reframing post-ECT confusion as predominantly transient. The study also found that the anaesthetic used matters: patients given thiopental or etomidate were significantly less likely to become confused than those given propofol, suggesting an underappreciated variable in ECT protocols. Why it fits: ECT is experiencing a reputational rehabilitation in public discourse, and NS Mind readers interested in mental health treatments would want to understand both the risks and their limits.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, outcome assessors not blinded. Small single-centre trial (N=90) in India limits generalisability; outcome assessors were not blinded, introducing potential bias; exploratory regression analysis should be treated as hypothesis-generating; authors themselves call for larger multicentre replication *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract states participants were blinded to treatment allocation but outcome assessors were not — noted as a design limitation (partial blinding). N=90 confirmed. Delirium rates and OR values verified against abstract. Study conducted in India — noted in summary as relevant context for single-centre setting.*

studies.title: Stigma and mistrust — not lack of awareness — are the main barriers stopping gay and bisexual men from taking HIV prevention pills
studies.ns_score_reason: Relevant public health topic with a clear societal hook, but a small scoping review of 13 studies with no counterintuitive finding and limited new empirical data keeps the score modest for NS Mind.
studies.the_study: Researchers at Western Sydney University conducted a scoping review of 13 studies published between 2015 and 2025, examining factors influencing PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) uptake and adherence among men who have sex with men (MSM) globally. Using a Social-Ecological Model and Intersectionality Framework, they found that barriers included low perceived HIV risk, stigma, healthcare mistrust, limited provider engagement, and financial constraints. Intersecting social identities — including ethnicity, religion, relationship status, and socioeconomic status — shaped how these barriers operated, suggesting a one-size-fits-all approach to PrEP promotion is unlikely to reach the most marginalised groups.
studies.why_it_matters: Despite PrEP being highly effective at preventing HIV, uptake remains inequitable; this review suggests structural and identity-based factors — not just individual knowledge gaps — are driving the disparity, with implications for how public health campaigns are designed.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "Why knowing about HIV prevention pills isn't enough to make people take them" A global review finds that stigma, healthcare mistrust, and intersecting social disadvantages — not ignorance — are the main reasons gay and bisexual men don't take PrEP, the pill that is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV. PrEP has existed for over a decade and works almost perfectly, yet HIV rates among MSM remain disproportionately high. A new scoping review finds the bottleneck isn't awareness — it's a web of stigma, mistrust of doctors, and compounding disadvantages tied to race, religion, and income. The finding challenges public health campaigns that default to information-sharing, suggesting deeper structural change is needed. Why it fits: NS Mind readers care about health inequity and the psychology of health behaviour — this reframes PrEP access as a social and structural problem, not an information problem.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: small sample (13 studies reviewed), observational design, scoping review (not systematic meta-analysis), heterogeneous study populations. Only 13 studies were included and this is a scoping — not systematic — review, so no statistical pooling of effects was possible; findings are synthesised qualitatively and may not reflect the full global evidence base *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirms 13 eligible studies included in the review. Design is a scoping review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis — noted accurately in caveats. No quantitative pooling of effect sizes reported.*

studies.title: Babies don't learn to walk in a straight line — their locomotor paths are messy, individual, and surprisingly backwards at times
studies.ns_score_reason: Counterintuitive finding about non-linear infant development is interesting, but very small sample, observational design, and Brazilian-specific context limit generalisability and NS Mind appeal.
studies.the_study: Researchers in Brazil tracked locomotor development in 37 typically developing infants across two age cohorts (5–11 months, N=19; 9–15 months, N=18), using parent-recorded home free-play videos every two weeks. They mapped the emergence and transitions between six locomotor behaviours — including belly crawling, hands-and-knees crawling, and walking. The study found striking interindividual variability, with up to 15 distinct emergence pathways and 13 transition pathways across groups, and transitions moving in multiple directions, sometimes from more complex to less complex behaviours — suggesting locomotor development is non-linear and highly individualised.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings challenge the textbook view of infant motor development as a neat sequential progression, suggesting parents and clinicians should expect wide variation in how and when babies move through locomotor milestones.
studies.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "Babies sometimes 'unlearn' to walk — infant locomotion is far messier than we thought" New research suggests that babies don't progress neatly from crawling to walking — they frequently regress to earlier movement patterns, and no two infants follow the same path. The standard picture of infant motor development — belly crawl, hands-and-knees crawl, pull to stand, walk — turns out to be a gross oversimplification. A Brazilian study tracking 37 infants at home found up to 15 different emergence pathways and frequent 'backward' transitions, with some babies temporarily reverting from more to less complex movements. This challenges decades of stage-based developmental theory and has implications for how parents and health visitors interpret milestone variation. Why it fits: NS Mind readers with children or an interest in developmental psychology would find this directly relatable and counterintuitive.
studies.wider_angle: Not generated by the previous pipeline.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes. Very small sample (N=37), single country (Brazil), parent-recorded videos introduce variability, observational design only — findings need replication in larger and more diverse samples *Editor's fact-check note: Sample sizes confirmed from abstract: Group 1 N=19, Group 2 N=18, total N=37. 'Self-reported outcomes' flagged because data was parent-generated video recordings, which introduces observer variability though it is naturalistic observation rather than self-report in the traditional sense — retained as a caveat given the non-standardised data collection.*
